occurring or extending throughout a state

s.d: Happening in or affecting an entire state (political subdivision of a federal union).

Fewer Saxon and Bavarian cities attempted to implement mandatory stunning laws, but their state parliaments debated the possibility of creating statewide bans on kosher butchering.

s.d: Happening in or affecting an entire sovereign state; nationwide.
x: Along with the rise of modern states came the establishment of statewide official currencies with the aim of protecting the corresponding markets and increasing trade within state territories.

s.d: Throughout a state (political subdivision of a federal union).

s.d: Throughout a sovereign state; nationwide.

s.d: a crackling or hissing noise caused by electrical interference
angry criticism
x: they will probably give you a lot of static about your editorial

s.d: (uncountable) Interference on a broadcast signal caused by atmospheric disturbances; heard as crackles on radio, or seen as random specks on television.
x: Near-synonyms: shash, snow
The World Series was on, but there was so much static that we could barely even follow the action.

s.d: (figuratively, uncountable) Interference or obstruction from people.
x: I was getting a lot of static from the bean counters whenever I tried to proceed.

s.d: (US, slang, uncountable) Verbal abuse.
x: Near-synonym: flak
Don't you be giving me any static over it. You know the rules.

s.d: (uncountable) Static electricity.
x: This stupid carpet is always giving me a shock from the static.

s.d: A static caravan.
A static variable.
x: Some compilers will allow statics to be inlined, but then incorrectly create multiple instances of the inlined variable at run-time.

s.d: not in physical motion
x: She remained motionless, yet poised to take flight

s.d: concerned with or producing or caused by static electricity
x: an electrostatic generator produces high-voltage static electricity

s.d: showing little if any change
x: a static population

s.d: Unchanging; that cannot or does not change.
x: It's important to know that the Earth's crust is in no manner a stable and static place.

s.d: Making no progress; stalled, without movement or advancement.
Immobile; fixed in place; having no motion.
x: England were ponderous with ball in hand, their runners static when taking the ball and their lines obvious, while their front row struggled badly in the scrum.

s.d: Computed, created, or allocated before the program starts running, as opposed to at runtime.
x: A further advantage of static type checking is of course computational efficiency, since run time checks are no longer necessary.
A static variable is one whose storage remains allocated for the duration of the entire program. All global variables are static variables.

s.d: Defined for the class itself, as opposed to instances of it; thus shared between all instances and accessible even without an instance.
electricity produced by friction
(uncountable) An electric charge that has built up on an insulated body, often due to friction.
(uncountable) The electric discharge from such a body.
(uncountable) Electrostatics.

a cord used instead of a ripcord to open a parachute; the cord is attached at one end to the aircraft and temporarily attached to the pack of a parachute at the other; it opens the parachute after the jumper is clear of the plane
The cord attached from the parachute pack to the plane, used to automatically deploy the parachute.
a magnet that retains its magnetism after being removed from a magnetic field
a measuring instrument used to measure static pressure in a stream of fluid

statice.e: From Latin staticē, from Ancient Greek στατικός (statikós, “standing still”).

s.d: any of various plants of the genus Limonium of temperate salt marshes having spikes of white or mauve flowers
the branch of mechanics concerned with forces in equilibrium

statin.e: From the suffix -statin, which was used for inhibiting hormone names before it was used for HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor drug names (but, like statin, has since become much better known in the latter sense).

s.d: a medicine that lowers blood cholesterol levels by inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase
Any of a class of drugs, the HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors, that lower the amount of cholesterol in the blood by inhibiting an enzyme involved in its biosynthesis.
x: Among the latest are reports of the ability of several leading statins to reduce deaths from common cancers and blunt the decline of memory with age.

s.d: An inhibiting hormone: a hormone that is involved primarily in inhibiting the release of another hormone.
a medicine that lowers blood cholesterol levels by inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase

station.e: From Middle English stacioun, borrowed from Anglo-Norman estation, from Latin statiōnem, accusative of statiō (“standing, post, job, position”), whence also Italian stazione. Doublet of stagione. Cognate with Ancient Greek ἵστημι (hístēmi), στάσις (stásis), Old English standan (whence English stand).

s.d: a facility equipped with special equipment and personnel for a particular purpose
x: he started looking for a gas station
the train pulled into the station

s.d: proper or designated social situation
x: he overstepped his place
the responsibilities of a man in his station

s.d: (nautical) the location to which a ship or fleet is assigned for duty
the position where someone (as a guard or sentry) stands or is assigned to stand
x: a soldier manned the entrance post
a sentry station

s.d: the frequency assigned to a broadcasting station
A stopping place.: A regular stopping place for ground transportation.
x: The next station is Esperanza.

s.d: A stopping place.: A place where one stands or stays or is assigned to stand or stay.
x: From my station at the front door, I greeted every visitor.
All ships are on station, Admiral.

s.d: A stopping place.: A place where some object is provided.
x: Collect a knife and fork from the cutlery station on the way to your table.

s.d: (US) A stopping place.: A gas station, service station.
A place where workers are stationed.: An official building from which police or firefighters operate.
x: The police station is opposite the fire station.

s.d: A place where workers are stationed.: A place where one performs a task or where one is on call to perform a task.
x: The waitress was at her station preparing three checks.
The station is part of a group of stations run by the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

s.d: A place where workers are stationed.: A military base.
x: She had a boyfriend at the station.
The dynamic tests at Wildenrath use continuous test tracks built on the site of a former Royal Air Force station that was vacated after the end of the Cold War.

s.d: A place where workers are stationed.: A place used for broadcasting radio or television; the broadcasting entity itself.
x: I used to work at a radio station.
I used to listen to that radio station.

s.d: A place where workers are stationed.: A device communicating over a network; a host.
x: An Econet network is made up of a number of stations.
When entering a LOAD/SAVE/FORMAT, etc command you not only had to identify the destination of the data (ie, microdrive, network or RS232), but the number of the drive or station too.

s.d: (Australia) A place where workers are stationed.: A very large sheep or cattle farm.

s.d: (historical) A place where workers are stationed.: In British India, the place where the English officials of a district, or the officers of a garrison (not in a fortress) reside.

s.d: the police sergeant on duty in a police station
a car that has a long body and rear door with space behind rear seat

station wagon.e: From train station; station wagons were originally designed for transporting people and luggage between stations and country estates.

s.d: a car that has a long body and rear door with space behind rear seat
(Australia, Canada, US) A body style for cars in which the roof is extended rearward to produce an enclosed area in the position and serving the function of the boot (trunk) of a sedan or saloon.

s.d: (obsolete) A vehicle (either horse-drawn or motorized) providing transport to and from a railway station for passengers and their luggage.

s.d: a branch of applied mathematics concerned with the collection and interpretation of quantitative data and the use of probability theory to estimate population parameters
(uncountable) A discipline, principally within applied mathematics, concerned with the systematic study of the collection, presentation, analysis, and interpretation of data.

English styrene
From Latin styrax (or storax) + -ene.

s.d: a colorless oily liquid; the monomer for polystyrene
An aromatic hydrocarbon; a colourless, oily liquid, used in the manufacture of polymers such as polystyrene.
x: He combined styrene with isobutylene, a volatile liquid, under pressure.
